FTIR spectra, TGA and SEM were used to characterize the origin and regenerated DAL. The origin and regenerated DAL shared the similar FTIR spectra disclosed in Fig. 11, where all the typical peaks of DAL were observed [76], indicating the negligible changes in the backbone structure of the regenerated DAL. Peaks at 1733, 1455, and 1263 were assigned to C=O stretching vibrations, C–H deformations absorption and ring breathing combined with C–O stretching respectively. The peaks at 1585 and 1510 cm⁻¹ were attributed to the vibration of the aromatic ring skeleton. 1122 and 1032 cm⁻¹ corresponded to the aromatic C–H in-plane deformation of syringyl and guaiacyl, respectively. Both the origin and regenerated lignin showed the fastest mass loss in the temperature range from 250 to 450 °C, due to the major devolatilization reactions [77]. However, after this stage, the regenerated lignin demonstrated a weaker thermal stability (45 wt% mass loss) than the origin lignin (35 wt% mass loss), indicating some changes occurred on the chemical structure of the regenerated DAL. Moreover, the maximum differential thermogravimetric value (DTGmax) of the regenerated DAL was 381 °C, much higher than that (340 °C) of origin DAL. This was because L-Pro/3FA facilitated the proton-catalyzed cleavage of lignin by interacting with eater links, resulting in the generation of lignin molecules with small molecular weight. But on the other hand, the inter/intra C–O and C–C bonds were formed after the cleavage of ether links, which required higher energy to be dissociated [78]. Through the SEM of the origin and re-generated DAL (Fig. 13), the surface of regenerated DAL seemed more rougher and polyporous, while the original DAL showed a more homo-geneous architecture. Conclusions In this study, we explored the synergistic effects of different functional groups in DESs on the lignin dissolving ability and further elaborate the lignin solubilization mechanism from the view of molecular interactions by using FTIR, and K-T Solvatochromic Parameters and DFT calculations. The theoretical and spectroscopic investigation revealed that the macroscopic dissolution behavior was due to the newly formed hydrogen bond between lignin and DESs along with the looser structure of lignin. The detailed research on structure-property-lignin dissolving ability of DESs indicated that functional groups of HBD and HBA and their molar ratio showed a vital role on the hydrogen bond interactions within DESs, reflected by the macroscopic property including viscosity and Solvatochromic property, which primarily determined the ability of DESs to form hydrogen bond with lignin. One hydroxyl and one carboxyl group played a positive role in lignin dissolution, due to the ability of providing active proton to form hydrogen bond with lignin. Conversely, the superfluous functional group such as the guanidine group in L-Arg and carbonyl group in LecA leaded to more complex hydrogen bond network and extensive dimer chains, thus resulting in the high viscosity of DESs and low lignin solubility. Moreover, the lignin solubility in the investigated DESs showed a positive correlation with K-T parameters α and π* and a closer positive correlation with the value of α-β, indicating that the donating hydrogen ability played a more important role on lignin dissolution. Among all the investigated DESs, L-Pro/3FA and L-Ala/3FA gave the high DAL solubility of 22.20 and 23.99 wt% at 60 °C, due to the low viscosity and strong net hydrogen-bond donating ability. More importantly, the global ESP maxima and minima of the DESs was positively associated the value of α and β of corresponding DESs, indicating the analysis of ESP quantitative distributions of DESs could provide guidance for designing effective lignin-dissolving DESs or other task-specific DES. ## Declaration of competing interest The authors declare that they have no known competing financial interests or personal relationships that could have appeared to influence the work reported in this paper.
